title: Java Memory Model evolution: pre-Java 5 broken, JSR-133, Java 9 VarHandle, Java 21
shortTitle: How has the Java Memory Model evolved?
keyPoints: Pre-Java 5 JMM was broken: volatile did not prevent reordering, double-checked locking was unsafe, and final fields had no visibility guarantee.
Java 5 (JSR-133) fixed everything: volatile provides full happens-before, final fields freeze at constructor end, and happens-before rules were formalized.
Java 5 also introduced java.util.concurrent with Executors, Locks, Atomics, and ConcurrentHashMap.
Java 9 added VarHandle with fine-grained memory access modes: plain, opaque, acquire/release, and volatile, replacing sun.misc.Unsafe.
Acquire/release semantics on VarHandle are cheaper than full volatile on ARM and POWER architectures.
Java 21 introduced virtual threads (lightweight, millions possible) and removed biased locking.
Application developers should stick with volatile and synchronized; VarHandle is for framework and library authors.

s1_definition.oneliner: The JMM evolved from a broken pre-Java 5 model (unsafe DCL, unreliable volatile) to JSR-133 in Java 5 (full happens-before), Java 9 (VarHandle with fine-grained access modes), and Java 21 (virtual threads, biased locking removed).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Pre-Java 5** – the original JMM was underspecified. `volatile` prevented caching but did not prevent instruction reordering. Double-checked locking was broken because the JVM could publish an object reference before the constructor completed. `final` fields had no cross-thread visibility guarantee: another thread could see a final field as null or zero.
- **Java 5 (JSR-133)** – completely rewrote the memory model. Volatile now provides a full happens-before edge that prevents reordering. Final fields are frozen at constructor completion and guaranteed visible to any thread that sees the object reference. The happens-before framework was formally defined. `java.util.concurrent` was introduced.
- **Java 9 (VarHandle)** – added `java.lang.invoke.VarHandle` with four memory access modes: plain (no ordering), opaque (no tearing), acquire/release (one-directional barriers), and volatile (full ordering). This replaced `sun.misc.Unsafe` for low-level atomic operations.
- **Java 21** – virtual threads (lightweight threads managed by the JVM, blocking is cheap), biased locking removed (the single-thread lock optimization was too complex for diminishing returns on modern hardware).
s1_definition.analogy: Before Java 5, National Bank of India had no official rules for sharing information between tellers. Each teller's personal notepad might show different balances even when one teller had updated the shared ledger. Java 5 was the regulatory reform: official rules were published that said, "When you stamp the ledger (volatile write), every other teller reading the ledger (volatile read) must see your updates." Java 9 gave expert tellers finer tools: "I only need other tellers in this region to see my update (acquire/release), not everyone in every branch (full volatile)." Java 21 introduced freelance tellers (virtual threads) who cost almost nothing to hire and can wait on hold without blocking a desk.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The JMM evolved from a broken pre-Java 5 model where volatile did not prevent reordering, double-checked locking was unsafe, and final fields had no visibility guarantee, to the robust JSR-133 specification in Java 5 that introduced full happens-before semantics for volatile, final field freeze at constructor end, and the formal happens-before framework. Java 5 also brought java.util.concurrent with Executors, Locks, Atomics, and ConcurrentHashMap.

Java 9 added VarHandle with four memory access modes (plain, opaque, acquire/release, volatile), giving framework authors fine-grained control over memory ordering. Acquire/release is cheaper than full volatile on ARM and POWER architectures, which matters for lock-free algorithms in high-performance systems. Java 21 introduced virtual threads that make blocking IO cheap (JVM unmounts virtual thread from carrier) and removed biased locking.

At National Bank of India, upgrading from Java 1.4 to Java 5 eliminated a once-per-month NullPointerException caused by broken DCL in the connection pool singleton. The volatile keyword on the instance field was all it took. Java 21 virtual threads later allowed the payment gateway to handle 100,000 concurrent API requests on the same hardware.

Remember one sentence: the JMM went from broken (pre-5) to fixed (JSR-133) to fine-grained (VarHandle) to lightweight (virtual threads), and for application code volatile plus synchronized is still the right choice.
